title: Ch 6: Link Layer Introduction and Error Detection

questions.q: In link-layer terminology, what is a layer-2 packet called?
questions.explain: A layer-2 packet is a frame. It encapsulates a network-layer datagram.

questions.q: What is the link layer responsible for?
choices: Transferring a datagram from one node to a physically adjacent node over a link
Delivering a segment from a process on one host to a process on another host
Choosing the end-to-end path a datagram takes from source to destination
Translating hostnames into IP addresses
questions.explain: The link layer works one hop at a time. It moves a datagram across a single link between physically adjacent nodes. End-to-end path selection is routing, which is a network-layer job.

questions.q: In link-layer terminology, both hosts and routers are called nodes, and the communication channels connecting adjacent nodes along the path are called links.
questions.explain: Hosts and routers are nodes. Links are the channels that connect adjacent nodes along a communication path, and they can be wired, wireless, or LANs.

questions.q: A trip from Princeton to Lausanne uses a limo to JFK, a plane to Geneva, and a train to Lausanne. In the analogy to the link layer, what does the mode of transportation on each leg (limo, plane, train) correspond to?
choices: A link-layer protocol
A datagram
A routing algorithm
A communication link
questions.explain: Transportation mode = link-layer protocol. Tourist = datagram, each transport segment = communication link, travel agent = routing algorithm.

questions.q: In the same travel analogy (limo, plane, train from Princeton to Lausanne), what does the travel agent who plans the whole trip correspond to?
choices: A routing algorithm
A link-layer protocol
A frame
A network interface card
questions.explain: The travel agent plans the whole route, just as a routing algorithm decides the end-to-end path. Each leg is then carried out by its own transport mode, which corresponds to a link-layer protocol.

questions.q: A datagram has to be carried by the same link-layer protocol on every link along its path.
questions.explain: Different link protocols can carry the datagram over different links. For example, it might use WiFi on the first link and Ethernet on the next.

questions.q: Every link-layer protocol provides reliable data transfer over its link.
questions.explain: Each link protocol provides different services. Some provide reliable data transfer over the link and some do not.

questions.q: Which of the following are services that a link-layer protocol may provide?
choices: Framing: encapsulating a datagram with a header and trailer
Choosing the route a datagram takes from the source host to the destination host
Error detection
Flow control between adjacent sending and receiving nodes
Reliable delivery between adjacent nodes
Error correction
questions.explain: Link-layer services include framing and link access, reliable delivery between adjacent nodes, flow control, error detection, error correction, and half/full-duplex operation. End-to-end route selection is a network-layer (routing) function.

questions.q: Link-layer frame headers carry "MAC" addresses. What do these addresses do?
choices: Identify the frame's source and destination; they are different from IP addresses
Give the datagram's source and destination IP addresses
Identify the application process that sent the data
Identify the router that computed the end-to-end route
questions.explain: MAC addresses in frame headers identify the source and destination at the link layer. They are not the same as IP addresses.

questions.q: Besides framing, the link layer may need to provide channel (link) access. When is that needed?
choices: When the medium is shared by multiple nodes
Only when the link uses fiber
Only when the frame carries a TCP segment
Whenever the frame has a bit error
questions.explain: Framing and link access includes channel access when the medium is shared, so nodes must coordinate their use of the channel.

questions.q: Why is link-level reliable delivery seldom used on some links but common on wireless links?
choices: Links with low bit-error rates rarely need it, while wireless links have high error rates
Wireless links cannot carry frame headers
Wired links already correct every error in hardware, so errors never occur
Reliable delivery only works when the medium is not shared
questions.explain: Reliable delivery between adjacent nodes is seldom used on low bit-error links. Wireless links have high error rates, so it is worthwhile there.

questions.q: Why can it make sense to have both link-level reliability (for example, on a wireless hop) and end-to-end reliability?
choices: On a high-error link, fixing errors at that hop avoids relying only on slower end-to-end retransmission, but other links on the path may not provide reliability, so the endpoints still need it
Link-level reliability guarantees that no errors can occur anywhere on the path, so end-to-end reliability only adds overhead
End-to-end reliability works only on wired links, so wireless links must replace it
The two are the same mechanism implemented twice for redundancy, with no difference in scope
questions.explain: Link-level reliability covers only one link, and each link protocol may or may not provide it. So it cannot replace end-to-end reliability. On a high-error link such as wireless, though, retransmitting at that hop recovers locally and quickly.

questions.q: What distinguishes error correction from error detection?
choices: With error correction, the receiver identifies and corrects bit errors without a retransmission
Error correction only checks the header, not the data
Error correction always requires the sender to retransmit the frame
Error correction drops the frame instead of signaling a retransmission
questions.explain: With error detection, the receiver finds errors and then signals for a retransmission or drops the frame. With error correction, the receiver identifies and fixes the bit errors itself, without a retransmission.

questions.q: A receiver detects a bit error in a frame that it cannot correct. What may it do?
choices: Signal the sender to retransmit
Drop the frame
Re-route the frame along a different path
Pass the datagram up as if it were valid
questions.explain: When a receiver detects errors, it either signals a retransmission or drops the frame.

questions.q: What causes the bit errors that link-layer error detection is designed to catch?
choices: Signal attenuation and noise
Routing loops
Incorrect MAC addresses in the header
Full transport-layer receive buffers
questions.explain: Bit errors on a link are caused by signal attenuation and noise.

questions.q: What does link-layer flow control do?
choices: Paces transmission between adjacent sending and receiving nodes
Picks the least congested end-to-end path
Corrects flipped bits in the frame
Assigns MAC addresses to interfaces
questions.explain: Link-layer flow control paces the sender so it doesn't overwhelm the receiving node at the other end of the link.

questions.q: On a half-duplex link, which statement is true?
choices: Nodes at both ends can transmit, but not at the same time
Only one end of the link can ever transmit
Both ends can transmit at the same time
Each frame must be sent twice
questions.explain: With half duplex, both ends can transmit, but they take turns. With full duplex, both can transmit at the same time.

questions.q: Where is the link layer implemented in a host?
choices: On-chip or in a network interface card (NIC)
Only in the router the host is attached to
Only in the application
Only in the host's transport-layer code
questions.explain: Every host has a link layer, implemented on-chip or in a network interface card (NIC).

questions.q: Which layers does a network interface card (NIC) implement?
choices: Application
Transport
Network
Link
Physical
questions.explain: The NIC (its controller plus physical-layer hardware) implements the link and physical layers. The CPU and memory run the upper layers.

questions.q: The link layer in a host is implemented purely in hardware.
questions.explain: The link layer is a combination of hardware, software, and firmware.

questions.q: The link layer is implemented in every host, not only in routers.
questions.explain: Every host has a link layer, either on-chip or in a NIC.

questions.q: How does a host's network interface connect to the rest of the host?
choices: It attaches to the host's system bus (e.g., PCI), which connects to the CPU and memory
It connects directly to the application through a socket
It attaches only to the physical cable and has no connection to the CPU
It is part of the CPU's instruction set
questions.explain: The network interface (controller plus physical layer) attaches to the host's system bus, such as PCI, which connects it to the CPU and memory.

questions.q: When two interfaces communicate, which of these tasks belong to the SENDING side?
choices: Encapsulates the datagram in a frame
Adds error-checking bits (plus reliable data transfer, flow control, etc.)
Extracts the datagram and passes it to the upper layer
Looks for errors in the incoming frame
questions.explain: The sender encapsulates the datagram in a frame and adds error-checking bits, reliable data transfer, flow control, etc. The receiver looks for errors and handles reliable transfer and flow control, then extracts the datagram and passes it up.

questions.q: After the receiving interface has checked a frame for errors, what does it do with a good frame?
choices: Extracts the datagram and passes it to the upper layer
Adds a new frame header and sends it back to the sender
Passes the whole frame, header included, to the application
Discards the datagram and keeps only the header
questions.explain: The receiving side looks for errors (and handles reliable data transfer, flow control, etc.), then extracts the datagram and passes it up to the network layer.

questions.q: In error-detection notation, what does EDC stand for?
choices: Error detection and correction bits (redundancy added to the data)
Encapsulated datagram content
End-to-end delivery confirmation
Ethernet destination code
questions.explain: EDC is the redundant error detection and correction bits sent along with the protected data D.

questions.q: The data D protected by error checking may include header fields, not just the payload.
questions.explain: D is the data protected by error checking, and it may include header fields.

questions.q: The sender transmits D and EDC, and the receiver works with D' and EDC'. Why the primes?
choices: They are the received versions, which may differ from what was sent because the link is bit-error prone
They are the corrected versions produced by the sender
They are copies the sender keeps for retransmission
They are the header fields only
questions.explain: The link can flip bits, so what arrives (D', EDC') may differ from what was sent (D, EDC). The receiver checks whether all bits in D' are OK.

questions.q: If the receiver's error check on D' and EDC' passes, the received data is guaranteed to be error-free.
questions.explain: Error detection is not 100% reliable. The protocol can occasionally miss errors.

questions.q: What is the general effect of using a larger EDC field?
choices: Better error detection and correction
Errors become impossible to miss
Less overhead per frame
No effect; only the algorithm matters
questions.explain: A larger EDC field gives better detection and correction, though detection still isn't 100% reliable.

questions.q: What can a single parity bit detect?
choices: Single bit errors
Any number of bit errors
Single bit errors, and it can also correct them
All burst errors up to the length of the data
questions.explain: A single parity bit detects single bit errors. Detecting and correcting single bit errors takes two-dimensional parity.

questions.q: Using EVEN parity, what parity bit should be appended to the data bits 11010011?
questions.explain: 11010011 contains five 1s. Even parity needs an even total number of 1s, so the parity bit is 1.

questions.q: Using ODD parity, what parity bit should be appended to the data bits 01100111?
questions.explain: 01100111 contains five 1s, which is already odd, so the parity bit is 0.

questions.q: Even parity is in use. A receiver gets the data bits 1001101 followed by the parity bit 1. What should it conclude?
choices: An error is detected
No error is detected
The error is detected and the flipped bit can be identified
Nothing; the parity bit is ignored at the receiver
questions.explain: The data has four 1s, so even parity should give a parity bit of 0. The receiver computes parity over the received data bits and compares it with the received parity bit. They differ, so an error is detected. A single parity bit can't tell which bit flipped.

questions.q: With single-bit even parity, if exactly two bits flip in transit, the receiver will detect the error.
questions.explain: Two flips change the count of 1s by 0 or 2, so the count stays even and the parity check still passes. That is why single parity is described as detecting single bit errors.

questions.q: Two-dimensional parity can both detect and correct a single bit error without a retransmission.
questions.explain: In two-dimensional parity, the data is arranged in rows and columns with a parity bit for each row and each column. A single flipped bit causes exactly one row check and one column check to fail, which pinpoints the bit so it can be flipped back.

questions.q: In two-dimensional parity, how does the receiver find a single flipped bit?
choices: It is at the intersection of the row and the column whose parity checks fail
It is always the last bit of the row that fails
It is found by dividing the block by a generator
It can't be found; the frame must be retransmitted
questions.explain: One row parity error plus one column parity error identifies a single cell, and that cell holds the flipped bit.

questions.q: Two-dimensional EVEN parity, 3 rows x 4 data columns. Each row is shown as data|row-parity, and the last line is the column-parity row. Received: row 1 = 1100|0, row 2 = 0101|1, row 3 = 1010|0, column parity = 0001|1. Which data bit is in error?
choices: Row 2, column 3
Row 2, column 2
Row 3, column 3
Row 1, column 4
questions.explain: Row checks: row 1 has two 1s (ok), row 2 has 0+1+0+1+1 = three 1s (fails), row 3 has two 1s (ok). Column checks: column 3 has 0+0+1 plus parity 0 = one 1 (fails), and all other columns are even. The error is at row 2, column 3, so the received 0 should be 1.

questions.q: When computing the Internet checksum, how does the sender treat the contents of the segment?
choices: As a sequence of 16-bit integers
As a sequence of 8-bit characters
As one large binary number to be divided by a generator
As a 2-D array of bits with row and column parity
questions.explain: The sender treats the segment contents as a sequence of 16-bit integers and adds them up.

questions.q: How is the Internet checksum computed?
choices: Addition (one's complement sum) of the segment content
Modulo-2 polynomial division by a generator G
Computing a parity bit for each row and column
XOR of the source and destination MAC addresses
questions.explain: The checksum is a one's complement sum of the segment content, and the result goes into the UDP checksum field. Division by a generator is how CRC works.

questions.q: For UDP, which of the following are included when the sender computes the checksum?
choices: The UDP segment's data
The UDP header fields
The IP addresses
The link-layer frame trailer
questions.explain: The sender treats the contents of the UDP segment, including the UDP header fields and the IP addresses, as 16-bit integers. The link-layer trailer is added later, at a lower layer.

questions.q: The receiver computes the checksum of a received segment, and it does NOT equal the value in the checksum field. What does this mean?
choices: An error has been detected
No error has been detected
The error has been corrected
The checksum field should be ignored
questions.explain: If the values are not equal, an error has been detected. If they are equal, no error is detected, but errors might still be present.

questions.q: If the receiver's computed checksum equals the checksum field, the segment definitely contains no errors.
questions.explain: A match only means no error was detected. Some errors can leave the checksum unchanged.

questions.q: A CRC uses r CRC bits. How many bits long is the generator G?
choices: r
2r
questions.explain: G is a bit pattern of r+1 bits, specified in the CRC standard. It produces r CRC bits.

questions.q: A CRC uses the generator G = 10011. How many CRC bits (r) does the sender append to the data?
questions.explain: G has r+1 bits. G is 5 bits, so r = 4.

questions.q: In the formula <D,R> = D·2^r XOR R, what does multiplying D by 2^r do?
choices: Shifts D left by r bit positions, leaving r zero bits at the end where R goes
Doubles each bit of D
Appends a copy of D to itself r times
Converts D to a one's complement number
questions.explain: D·2^r is D with r zeros appended. XORing with R then fills those r positions with the CRC bits, giving the d+r bits that are sent.

questions.q: How does the sender choose the r CRC bits R?
choices: So that <D,R> is exactly divisible by G using modulo-2 arithmetic
So that the number of 1s in <D,R> is even
So that R is the one's complement sum of D
So that D + R equals G
questions.explain: The sender picks R so that <D,R> divides exactly by G (mod 2). The receiver knows G and can check this.

questions.q: Starting from D·2^r XOR R = nG, which is equivalent to D·2^r = nG XOR R, how does the sender actually compute R?
choices: R = remainder of (D·2^r) / G, using modulo-2 division
R = quotient of (D·2^r) / G
R = D XOR G
R = remainder of D / 2^r
questions.explain: D·2^r = nG XOR R says that dividing D·2^r by G leaves R as the remainder. So the sender appends r zeros to D, divides by G mod 2 (XOR at each step, no carries), and takes the r-bit remainder.

questions.q: The receiver divides the received <D,R> by G. What does a non-zero remainder mean?
choices: An error was detected
No error occurred
The error was corrected
The generator was wrong and should be replaced
questions.explain: A correctly received <D,R> divides exactly by G. A non-zero remainder means an error was detected.

questions.q: A CRC uses r = 8 CRC bits. What is the length, in bits, of the longest burst error it is guaranteed to detect?
questions.explain: A CRC detects all burst errors shorter than r+1 bits. With r = 8 that means bursts shorter than 9 bits, so up to 8 bits.

questions.q: Which of the following use CRC for error detection?
choices: Ethernet
802.11 WiFi
UDP's segment error check
questions.explain: CRC is widely used in link technologies such as Ethernet and 802.11 WiFi. UDP uses the Internet checksum (a one's complement sum).

questions.q: Compute the CRC bits R for data D = 101101 and generator G = 1101. Give R as a bit string of length r.
questions.explain: G has 4 bits, so r = 3. D·2^3 = 101101000. Mod-2 division by 1101: 1011 XOR 1101 = 0110; bring down 0: 1100 XOR 1101 = 0001; bring down 1: 0011 (leading 0, quotient bit 0); bring down 0: 0110 (quotient bit 0); bring down 0: 1100 XOR 1101 = 0001; bring down 0: 0010 (quotient bit 0). The remainder is R = 010.

questions.q: For data D = 101101 and generator G = 1101, what full bit string <D,R> does the sender transmit?
questions.explain: r = 3 and R = remainder(101101000 / 1101) = 010. Sent bits = D followed by R = 101101010, which divides exactly by 1101.

questions.q: Compute the CRC bits R for data D = 110101 and generator G = 101. Give R as a bit string of length r.
questions.explain: G has 3 bits, so r = 2. D·2^2 = 11010100. Mod-2 division by 101: 110 XOR 101 = 011; bring down 1: 111 XOR 101 = 010; bring down 0: 100 XOR 101 = 001; bring down 1: 011 (quotient bit 0); bring down 0: 110 XOR 101 = 011; bring down 0: 110 XOR 101 = 011. The remainder is R = 11, and the sender transmits 11010111.

questions.q: With generator G = 1001, a receiver gets the bits 101010011. What remainder does it get, and what does it conclude?
choices: Remainder 100: error detected
Remainder 000: no error detected
Remainder 011: no error detected
Remainder 000: error detected
questions.explain: Mod-2 division by 1001: 1010 XOR 1001 = 0011; bring down 1: 0111 (quotient bit 0); bring down 0: 1110 XOR 1001 = 0111; bring down 0: 1110 XOR 1001 = 0111; bring down 1: 1111 XOR 1001 = 0110; bring down 1: 1101 XOR 1001 = 0100. The remainder is 100, which is non-zero, so an error is detected. (The valid codeword for D = 101110 is 101110011; one bit flipped.)
